title: When Results Refuse to Repeat: Replication and the Credibility of Science
skill_tip_en: For inference questions, connect two or more pieces of evidence, often from different sentences, and choose the option the text supports without stating it, rejecting options that merely recycle the passage's wording or go further than the evidence allows.
paragraphs: Few principles are recited more confidently in introductory science courses than the claim that a finding becomes knowledge only when others can reproduce it. A single experiment, however elegant, is regarded as provisional: its results may reflect chance, an unnoticed flaw in the equipment or the particular habits of one laboratory. Replication is supposed to filter out such accidents. Yet over the past fifteen years, a series of large-scale attempts to repeat published studies has suggested that this filter works far less reliably than textbooks imply. In some fields, fewer than half of the re-run experiments produced results resembling the originals, a pattern now widely described as the “replication crisis”.

The causes most often cited are statistical rather than moral. Many studies, particularly in psychology and the biomedical sciences, rely on small samples, which makes them prone to detecting effects that are either exaggerated or entirely spurious. This weakness is compounded by publication bias: journals have traditionally favoured striking, positive results, while studies that find nothing tend to remain in researchers’ filing cabinets. As a consequence, the published literature may represent a skewed sample of all the research actually conducted. If twenty teams test the same ineffective treatment and one obtains a “significant” result by chance, it is that one result, not the nineteen failures, that is most likely to reach print.

A further difficulty is what methodologists call analytical flexibility. A researcher analysing a dataset faces dozens of defensible choices: which participants to exclude, which variables to control for, when to stop collecting data. Each choice may seem innocent in isolation, but taken together they allow almost any dataset to be coaxed into yielding a publishable pattern. Crucially, this need not involve deliberate dishonesty. Dr. Pimchanok Saelee, a methodologist at a university in northern Thailand, argues that most such decisions are made in good faith by scientists who sincerely believe they are uncovering a real effect. “The danger,” she notes, “is not fraud but optimism operating under pressure to publish.”

Not everyone accepts that the situation amounts to a crisis. Some philosophers of science point out that a failed replication is itself an experimental result, subject to exactly the same uncertainties as the original. A repeat study may differ from the first in subtle ways — a different population, a translated questionnaire, a change of season — that alter the outcome without either study being wrong. On this view, low replication rates may partly reflect the genuine context-sensitivity of certain phenomena, particularly in the social sciences, where human behaviour is shaped by culture and circumstance. Admittedly, this argument has limits: if an effect vanishes whenever conditions change slightly, its practical and theoretical significance is questionable.

In response to these concerns, a number of reforms have gained ground. The most prominent is pre-registration, in which researchers publicly record their hypotheses and analysis plans before collecting data, thereby limiting the scope for flexible analysis after the fact. Some journals have gone further by adopting “registered reports”, agreeing to publish a study on the basis of its design, regardless of whether the eventual results are positive. Early evidence is encouraging: a 2023 comparison of several hundred papers found that registered reports presented supportive results far less often than conventional articles did, which suggests that the format is removing at least some of the distortion introduced by selective publication.

These measures are not without costs. Critics warn that rigid pre-registration may discourage exploratory research, in which scientists follow unexpected leads that no plan could have anticipated, and they observe that much of the history of discovery consists of precisely such detours. Others note that repeating studies is time-consuming and poorly rewarded; a young researcher who spends two years confirming someone else’s finding may discover that hiring committees value the effort far less than an original, if fragile, discovery. Unless funding bodies and universities change what they reward, the burden of replication is likely to fall on those least able to bear it.

Perhaps the most valuable lesson of the replication debate is philosophical rather than technical. It has reminded scientists that certainty in science is accumulated slowly and collectively, not delivered by any single study, however prestigious the journal in which it appears. Seen in this light, the discovery that many findings do not survive repetition is less an indictment of science than evidence that its self-correcting mechanisms, though slower than once assumed, are still functioning. The challenge now is to make that correction routine rather than exceptional.

options: Replication failures prove that most published science is unreliable and should be disregarded.
Difficulties in reproducing findings expose weak research practices, yet science can still correct itself.

Philosophers have shown that the replication crisis is an illusion created by differences in context.

title: Thinking Fast in the Shopping Aisle: The Quiet Power of Mental Shortcuts
focus: author's stance and tone (tone, purpose, fact/opinion)
skill_tip_en: To identify the author's stance, look for evaluative words and phrases (frankly, naive, hardly, unfortunately, deserves to be taken seriously) and for concessions, and separate the claims the author merely reports from the claims the author endorses.
paragraphs: Every day, most of us make hundreds of small decisions — which queue to join, which brand of rice to buy, whether to renew a gym membership we rarely use. We like to believe that these choices are the product of careful deliberation. A substantial body of research suggests otherwise. Much of our everyday decision-making relies on mental shortcuts, or heuristics, which allow us to act quickly on the basis of limited information. Such shortcuts are often useful; without them, we would be paralysed by trivial choices. But they also produce systematic errors, known as cognitive biases, that are predictable enough to be studied — and, increasingly, exploited.

Consider anchoring, the tendency to rely too heavily on the first number we encounter. In a 2022 experiment at a university in Khon Kaen, shoppers were shown a jacket with a “recommended price” before being asked what they would pay for it. Those who saw a recommended price of 2,400 baht offered, on average, nearly 40 per cent more than those who saw 1,200 baht, even though the jacket was identical. Retailers have long understood this effect, which is why so many price tags display a crossed-out figure above the sale price. That original figure, frankly, is often less a price than a piece of theatre.

Equally familiar is the sunk-cost fallacy: our reluctance to abandon something once we have invested time or money in it. People sit through dull films because they have paid for the tickets, and governments persist with failing infrastructure projects because too much has already been spent to stop. From a strictly economic standpoint, past costs that cannot be recovered should be irrelevant to future decisions. Psychologically, however, abandoning an investment feels like admitting a mistake, and few of us enjoy doing that. It would be naive to imagine that institutions are immune; if anything, the public nature of their commitments makes retreat even harder.

Perhaps the most costly bias, at least for household finances, is present bias — the habit of giving disproportionate weight to immediate rewards over future ones. It helps to explain why many people intend to save for retirement yet repeatedly postpone doing so, and why “buy now, pay later” schemes have spread so rapidly among young consumers. A survey of 1,500 working adults in Bangkok, conducted in 2024 by a private research institute, found that 61 per cent had no retirement savings beyond the compulsory minimum, although most described saving as “very important”. The gap between what people value and what they actually do could hardly be wider.

It would be wrong, though, to conclude that human beings are simply irrational. Some researchers argue that many so-called biases are sensible responses to the environments in which our minds evolved, where information was scarce and quick decisions often mattered more than perfect ones. A heuristic that misleads us in a laboratory may serve us well in daily life. This argument deserves to be taken seriously, but it is sometimes stretched too far. The fact that a shortcut was once adaptive does not make it harmless in a modern marketplace designed by people who understand it better than we do.

What, then, can be done? Awareness alone, unfortunately, offers limited protection; studies repeatedly find that people who can define a bias are scarcely less susceptible to it. More promising are changes to the context in which choices are made. Automatically enrolling employees in pension schemes, while allowing them to opt out, has raised participation dramatically in several countries. Such nudges work with our biases rather than against them. Critics object that they are paternalistic, and the concern is not trivial: a technique that steers people towards saving can just as easily steer them towards spending.

The study of cognitive bias is sometimes presented as a catalogue of human foolishness. That is, I think, a mistake. Its real value lies in shifting the question from whether people are rational to how decisions can be designed so that ordinary, hurried, imperfect thinkers are more likely to choose well. We will never stop taking shortcuts. The task is to make sure that the roads they lead down are, more often than not, the ones we would have chosen if we had had time to think.

title: From Soil to Supper: Tracing Microplastics Through the Food Web
skill_tip_en: Paraphrased detail questions rarely repeat the passage's wording, so locate the relevant sentence, match its meaning rather than its vocabulary, and be wary of options that echo key words but change the relationship between them.
paragraphs: Microplastics — fragments of plastic smaller than five millimetres — were first documented as a marine pollutant, and for many years research focused almost exclusively on the oceans. That emphasis is now shifting. Scientists increasingly recognise that the food people eat may be contaminated not only through the sea but also through farmland, irrigation water and processing, and that the routes by which particles move between organisms are more varied than early studies assumed. Understanding these routes matters because the potential health consequences of dietary exposure depend less on whether microplastics are present, which is now beyond dispute, than on how much accumulates, where, and in what form.

The marine pathway remains the best documented. Filter-feeding animals such as mussels and oysters process large volumes of seawater and retain suspended particles, including plastics, in their tissues. Because these shellfish are usually eaten whole, digestive tract included, they represent a direct route into the human diet. Fish present a more complicated picture. Most particles ingested by fish are concentrated in the gut, which consumers generally discard, so the quantity reaching the edible muscle appears to be comparatively small. Small fish eaten whole, such as anchovies, are an important exception, and in parts of Southeast Asia they form a regular component of household meals.

Less attention has been paid to the land, although agricultural soils may now hold more microplastics than the oceans do. One major source is sewage sludge, which is valued by farmers as a cheap fertiliser but retains many of the synthetic fibres washed out of clothing. Plastic mulch films, used widely to suppress weeds and conserve moisture, add a further burden as they degrade under sunlight and are broken up during ploughing. Once in the soil, particles can be ingested by earthworms and other invertebrates, which are in turn eaten by birds and small mammals, linking contaminated fields to wider terrestrial food webs.

Whether crops themselves absorb microplastics has been a matter of considerable debate. For a long time it was assumed that particles were simply too large to pass through plant roots. However, laboratory experiments have shown that the very smallest fragments, known as nanoplastics, can enter the roots of lettuce and wheat through cracks that form where new lateral roots emerge, and may then be transported towards the leaves. A 2024 study at an agricultural university in central Thailand detected such particles in the leaves of hydroponically grown morning glory, a popular vegetable in the region, although the concentrations were low and the growing conditions differed considerably from those in an open field.

A central question is whether microplastics behave like certain persistent chemicals, such as mercury, that become more concentrated at each step up the food chain — a process known as biomagnification. The evidence so far is mixed. Particles are clearly transferred from prey to predator, but many also pass through the digestive system and are excreted rather than stored. Some researchers therefore argue that the more significant risk lies not in the plastic itself but in the chemicals it carries, including additives used in manufacturing and pollutants that adhere to particle surfaces in the environment.

Any assessment of exposure is complicated by serious methodological problems. Laboratories use different techniques to extract and identify particles, and their results are often not directly comparable. Contamination during analysis is a constant hazard: synthetic fibres from laboratory coats and from the air itself can find their way into samples, so careful studies must include blank controls to estimate background levels. Most importantly, the smallest particles, which may be the most biologically active, are also the hardest to detect, meaning that current estimates may understate rather than overstate exposure.

None of this justifies alarm at the dinner table, but neither does it justify complacency. The evidence indicates that microplastics enter the food chain through multiple routes, several of which were overlooked until recently. Reducing their flow at source — by restricting the use of contaminated sludge, improving the recovery of used mulch films and filtering fibres from domestic washing machines — is likely to prove more effective than attempting to remove particles from food after they have arrived. In the meantime, harmonising laboratory methods should be a priority, since policy can be no better than the measurements on which it is based.

title: Workers Without a Workplace: The Legal Puzzle of Platform Labour
focus: NOT/EXCEPT questions with true-but-unstated distractors (negative detail)
skill_tip_en: In NOT/EXCEPT questions, check every option against the passage and cross out each one that is actually stated; the correct answer often sounds perfectly true in the real world but simply does not appear in the text.
paragraphs: Over the past decade, digital platforms have transformed the way millions of people find paid work. Through a smartphone application, a person can deliver meals, drive passengers, clean homes or complete short online tasks, often within minutes of signing up. Some treat such work as a temporary supplement; for others, it has quietly become a full-time occupation. For workers, the attractions are real: flexible hours, low barriers to entry and the possibility of combining several sources of income. Yet the rapid growth of this “gig economy” has exposed a gap in labour law, which in most countries was designed around a simple distinction between employees, who receive protections such as a minimum wage and sick pay, and independent contractors, who do not.

Platform companies have generally classified their workers as independent contractors, arguing that they merely provide a technological marketplace connecting customers with self-employed service providers. Workers are free, the companies point out, to log in and out whenever they wish, to reject individual jobs and to work for competing platforms at the same time. Critics respond that this freedom is more limited than it appears. Algorithms frequently set prices, allocate tasks and evaluate performance through customer ratings, and workers whose acceptance rates fall below a certain level may find themselves receiving fewer offers or being deactivated altogether.

Courts in several jurisdictions have been asked to decide which description is more accurate. Their reasoning has typically focused on the degree of control a company exercises rather than on the label written in the contract. Where a platform determines the fare, monitors the route and disciplines workers through its rating system, judges have increasingly concluded that the relationship resembles employment in substance, whatever it is called on paper. Such rulings, however, apply only to the parties and facts before the court, and companies have often responded by adjusting their terms of service in ways that make subsequent cases harder to win.

Legislators have therefore explored more general solutions, which fall broadly into three models. The first creates an intermediate category of worker, entitled to some protections, such as minimum earnings and accident insurance, but not to the full set enjoyed by employees. The second establishes a legal presumption that platform workers are employees unless the company can prove otherwise, shifting the burden of evidence away from individual workers. The third leaves classification unchanged but requires platforms to contribute to social security funds or to disclose how their algorithms allocate work and calculate pay.

In Southeast Asia, where a large share of the workforce was informally employed long before platforms arrived, the debate takes a distinctive form. A 2025 survey of 2,000 delivery riders in three Thai cities, conducted by researchers at a public university in Bangkok, found that 58 per cent regarded platform work as their main source of income, and that fewer than a fifth had any accident insurance despite spending an average of nine hours a day on the road. Yet only a minority said they wished to become employees; most wanted better pay per delivery and clearer explanations when their accounts were suspended.

Opponents of stricter regulation warn that imposing employment obligations could raise costs, reduce the number of available jobs and remove the very flexibility that workers value. Some evidence supports this concern: in one European city, a platform that reclassified its couriers as employees subsequently introduced fixed shifts and reduced its workforce. However, the interpretation of such cases is contested, since companies may have reasons of their own to restructure, and the costs of leaving workers unprotected — borne by public hospitals, by families and by the workers themselves when accidents occur — rarely appear in such calculations.

What emerges from these debates is that the binary choice between employee and contractor may be the wrong starting point. Protections such as accident insurance, transparent pay and a fair process for challenging deactivation could be attached to the work itself rather than to a particular legal status. Designing such a system is not straightforward, and it will require platforms, governments and worker organisations to share data that they have so far guarded closely. But the alternative — leaving the rules to be settled one court case at a time — offers neither workers nor companies the certainty they need.

title: Sensing the City: Data, Surveillance and the Promise of Urban Intelligence
skill_tip_en: For organisation and purpose questions, ask what job each paragraph or example does in the argument (define, illustrate, concede, rebut or propose) rather than simply what it says, and use linking words such as Yet, Nevertheless and therefore to trace the structure.
paragraphs: The phrase “smart city” has become a fixture of urban planning documents across the world. In its broadest sense, it describes a city that uses networks of sensors, cameras and data platforms to monitor and manage its services, from traffic lights and street lighting to waste collection and water supply. Proponents present such systems as a means of making cities more efficient, sustainable and responsive to residents’ needs. Yet the same infrastructure that measures the flow of traffic can also record the movements of individuals, and the question of where efficient management ends and surveillance begins has become one of the defining dilemmas of contemporary urban governance.

The benefits claimed for smart-city technologies are not merely rhetorical. Sensors embedded in water pipes can detect leaks within hours rather than weeks, reducing losses that in some older networks exceed a third of the water supplied. Adaptive traffic signals, which adjust their timing according to real-time congestion, have shortened average journey times in a number of trials. In Thailand, several municipalities have installed air-quality monitors that issue alerts during the dry-season haze, allowing schools to keep children indoors on the worst days. Each of these applications relies on data, but much of that data concerns pipes, roads and air rather than people.

The difficulty arises when systems designed for one purpose acquire others. Scholars of surveillance use the term function creep to describe this gradual expansion. A camera network installed to enforce traffic regulations may later be connected to facial recognition software; data collected from public Wi-Fi to estimate pedestrian numbers may be shared with the police or sold to advertisers. Because each extension tends to be modest and is often justified on grounds of safety, the cumulative result can be a level of monitoring that no one explicitly approved and that residents may not even know exists.

The experience of a medium-sized city in the lower Mekong region illustrates the pattern. In 2019, its council installed 400 cameras at junctions to reduce accidents, a goal widely supported by residents. Within four years, the network had grown to more than 2,500 cameras, many fitted with licence-plate and face-matching capabilities, and footage was being retained for ninety days instead of the original seven. A 2024 study by researchers at a regional university found that fewer than one in ten residents were aware of these changes, although a majority said they would want to be consulted before such systems were expanded.

Defenders of smart-city surveillance argue that such concerns are exaggerated. They point out that people in public spaces have always been visible to others, that cameras can deter crime and assist investigations, and that many residents willingly share far more personal information with private technology companies than any city council collects. These arguments carry some weight, particularly where crime is a pressing local concern. Nevertheless, there is a difference between being seen by passers-by and being recorded, identified and stored by a single authority, since the latter allows patterns of behaviour — where a person worships, whom they meet, which clinic they visit — to be reconstructed long after the event.

If the benefits are to be secured without the risks, governance must keep pace with technology, and several measures have been proposed. Purpose limitation rules would require any new use of data to be approved separately rather than added quietly to an existing system. Independent oversight bodies, including members of the public, could review proposals before installation. Data minimisation — collecting only what is necessary and deleting it promptly — would reduce the harm that could follow a breach or misuse. Some cities have also experimented with public registers listing every sensor and camera, its purpose and the period for which its data are kept.

The smart city, then, is neither a utopia of seamless services nor an inevitable surveillance state. Its character depends on choices made by councils, companies and residents about what is measured, by whom and for what ends. The technologies themselves are largely neutral; the institutions that govern them are not. A city that wishes to be called smart in any meaningful sense must therefore be judged not only by the efficiency of its systems but also by the openness with which it explains them to the people they observe.

questions.q: What is the main function of paragraph 1?
options: To define the smart city and introduce the tension between management and surveillance
To argue that every smart city will inevitably develop into a surveillance state
To trace the history of urban planning documents over recent decades
To list the technologies that cities should avoid installing in public spaces
questions.explain: ¶1 ให้นิยาม (“In its broadest sense, it describes...”) แล้วเปิดประเด็นด้วย Yet ว่า “where efficient management ends and surveillance begins” เป็นปัญหาหลัก จึงตอบ A ตัวเลือก B ขัดกับ ¶7 ที่บอกว่า smart city “neither ... nor an inevitable surveillance state”

questions.q: Why does the author point out at the end of paragraph 2 that much of the data 'concerns pipes, roads and air rather than people'?
options: To argue that smart-city data is of little real value to residents
To indicate that these uses raise few privacy issues, preparing for a contrast
To show that sensors become unreliable when they are used to monitor people
To criticise municipalities for neglecting the needs of their residents
questions.explain: ¶2 ยกประโยชน์ที่ไม่เกี่ยวกับข้อมูลบุคคล แล้ว ¶3 เปิดด้วย “The difficulty arises when...” ประโยคท้าย ¶2 จึงทำหน้าที่ชี้ว่าการใช้งานเหล่านี้ไม่ค่อยกระทบความเป็นส่วนตัว และปูทางไปสู่ปัญหาใน ¶3 ตอบ B ตัวเลือก A ขัดกับ “The benefits ... are not merely rhetorical”

questions.q: The phrase 'this gradual expansion' in paragraph 3 refers to
options: the steady growth in the number of people living in cities
the rising influence of private technology companies
systems taking on uses beyond their original purpose
the spread of public Wi-Fi across city centres
questions.explain: ¶3: ประโยคก่อนหน้าคือ “systems designed for one purpose acquire others” ซึ่ง this gradual expansion ชี้กลับไป จึงตอบ C ตัวเลือก D ล่อใจเพราะ Wi-Fi ปรากฏในย่อหน้าเดียวกัน แต่เป็นเพียงตัวอย่างของการขยายการใช้งาน ไม่ใช่สิ่งที่วลีนี้อ้างถึง

questions.q: What is the relationship between paragraph 4 and paragraph 3?
options: Paragraph 4 contradicts the main claim made in paragraph 3.
Paragraph 4 proposes a solution to the problem raised in paragraph 3.
Paragraph 4 moves on to a topic unrelated to paragraph 3.
Paragraph 4 gives a concrete case of the process described in paragraph 3.
questions.explain: ¶4 เปิดด้วย “The experience of a medium-sized city ... illustrates the pattern” แล้วเล่าการขยายระบบกล้องจาก 400 เป็นกว่า 2,500 ตัว ซึ่งเป็นตัวอย่างของ function creep ใน ¶3 ตอบ D ตัวเลือก B ผิดเพราะแนวทางแก้ไขอยู่ใน ¶6 ไม่ใช่ ¶4

questions.q: What can be inferred from the 2024 study described in paragraph 4?
options: Residents strongly opposed the original installation of the cameras.
The network grew largely without meaningful public consultation.
Most residents wanted all of the cameras to be removed.
The cameras failed to reduce the number of road accidents.
questions.explain: ¶4: “fewer than one in ten residents were aware of these changes” แต่ส่วนใหญ่ “would want to be consulted” เมื่อคนแทบไม่รู้ จึงอนุมานได้ว่าไม่มีการปรึกษาประชาชนอย่างจริงจัง ตอบ B ตัวเลือก A กลับความหมาย เพราะเป้าหมายเดิม “widely supported by residents”

questions.q: Which of the following best describes how paragraph 5 is organised?
options: Opposing arguments are presented, partly accepted, and then answered with a key distinction.
The advantages of cameras are listed in order of their importance to residents.
Crime rates in cities with and without cameras are compared using statistics.
A problem is described and every proposed solution to it is then rejected.
questions.explain: ¶5 เริ่มด้วยข้อโต้แย้งของฝ่ายสนับสนุน ยอมรับบางส่วน (“These arguments carry some weight”) แล้วโต้กลับด้วย “Nevertheless, there is a difference between being seen ... and being recorded” จึงตอบ A ตัวเลือก B ล่อใจเพราะมีการระบุข้อดีของกล้อง แต่เป็นเพียงส่วนแรกของย่อหน้า

questions.q: Why does the author mention 'where a person worships, whom they meet, which clinic they visit' in paragraph 5?
options: To list places where the use of cameras is currently prohibited
To argue that companies collect more data than city councils
To show the sensitive patterns that stored recordings could reveal
To give examples of crimes that cameras have helped to solve
questions.explain: ¶5: ตัวอย่างเหล่านี้อธิบาย “patterns of behaviour” ที่สามารถ “be reconstructed long after the event” เมื่อภาพถูกบันทึกและเก็บไว้ จึงตอบ C ตัวเลือก B ล่อใจเพราะเป็นข้อโต้แย้งของฝ่ายสนับสนุนในย่อหน้าเดียวกัน ไม่ใช่จุดประสงค์ของตัวอย่างนี้

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the organisation of paragraph 6?
options: A chronological account of how one city regulated its camera network
A comparison of two opposing theories about surveillance in cities
A problem followed by evidence that existing safeguards have failed
A general principle followed by a series of proposed safeguards
questions.explain: ¶6 เริ่มด้วยหลักการ “governance must keep pace with technology” แล้วไล่มาตรการ purpose limitation, oversight bodies, data minimisation และ public registers จึงตอบ D ตัวเลือก C ผิดเพราะย่อหน้านี้เสนอมาตรการ ไม่ได้ให้หลักฐานว่ามาตรการล้มเหลว

questions.q: Which of the following statements would the author most likely agree with?
options: Smart-city technologies are inherently harmful and should be withdrawn.
A city's claim to be smart depends partly on how openly it governs data.
Efficiency is the only fair standard for judging a smart city.
Residents' opinions no longer matter once systems are installed.
questions.explain: ¶7: เมืองต้องถูกประเมิน “not only by the efficiency of its systems but also by the openness with which it explains them” จึงตอบ B ตัวเลือก C ล่อใจเพราะพูดถึงประสิทธิภาพ แต่ใช้คำว่า only ซึ่งขัดกับ not only ... but also และ A ขัดกับ “The technologies themselves are largely neutral”

questions.q: What term do scholars of surveillance use for the gradual expansion of a system beyond its original purpose? (Answer in NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶3: “Scholars of surveillance use the term function creep to describe this gradual expansion” คำตอบคือ function creep

questions.q: In the city described in paragraph 4, for how many days was camera footage originally retained? (Answer in NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶4: “footage was being retained for ninety days instead of the original seven” คำตอบคือ seven ไม่ใช่ ninety ซึ่งเป็นระยะเวลาหลังการขยายระบบ

questions.q: What measure involves collecting only the data that is necessary and deleting it promptly? (Answer in NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶6: “Data minimisation — collecting only what is necessary and deleting it promptly” คำตอบคือ data minimisation
